newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovan presidential candidates trade accusations.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan presidential candidates trade accusations.

text.p: The two remaining candidates in Moldova's presidential race traded accusations on Sunday as Moldovans went to the polls in the election runoff.
Challenger Petru Lucinschi accused President Mircea Snegur of planning to rig the vote. Snegur accused parliament speaker Lucinschi of running a dirty campaign.
"Unfortunately, I do not believe the elections will be completely fair," Lucinschi told reporters after voting in the capital, Chisinau.
"I have proof that people have been paid to vote. Other inventions to falsify the results are being used as well."
Lucinschi, whom polls put neck-and-neck with Snegur, also said he feared Snegur's supporters could take to the streets.
But there was no sign of tension in Chisinau in the early afternoon.
Observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) had reported no significant violations, although they have said the campaign was bitter.

Snegur, voting at the same polling station, accused his leftist challenger, who has been openly backed by state television bosses, of "illegal methods including mudslinging in the press, libel and rumours".
"The republic has been flooded with leaflets with lots of personal insults, and national television was practically put at Lucinschi's disposal," Snegur told reporters.
Late on Saturday, state television repeatedly broadcast an appeal from the Moldovan Orthodox Church to vote for Lucinschi.
"God bless you to summon up wisdom...and vote on December 1 for the swallow," Father Ioan, a spokesman for Metropolitan Vladimir, told viewers, referring to Lucinschi's campaign logo.
Lucinschi has said Snegur could use demonstrations and his influence over the police to destabilise Moldova if he loses.
"We have not yet adapted, like countries with democratic traditions, to meeting peacefully," he said. "Unfortunately, there are people saying they will not surrender."
Fighting with Russian-speaking separatists cost hundreds of lives in 1992. A constitutional stand-off between Snegur and Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli divided the army last March.
